title: Europe 6 of 6 · Baltic and Eastern Europe
edition: Europe countries · Six regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Europe episode six of six. First, I clear the chosen names so we can study a fresh regional group.
Our final nine-place group follows the Baltic countries south through Belarus and Ukraine, then Moldova, Romania and Bulgaria, finishing with European Russia.

states.name: Estonia
lines: Estonia is the northernmost Baltic country, directly south of Finland across the Gulf of Finland. Latvia is below it, and Russia lies to its east.
Estonian is closely related to Finnish. That language link points across the gulf, even though Estonia’s location groups it with Latvia and Lithuania.
Remember the Baltic stack from north to south: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. Estonia is the one facing Finland across the water.
states.transition: Let's bring Estonia and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Latvia
lines: Latvia is the middle Baltic country, below Estonia and above Lithuania. Its coastline bends around the Gulf of Riga, with Russia and Belarus toward the east.
Riga is renowned for its Art Nouveau buildings. Imagine decorative facades beside a Baltic trading port: a visual hook for the middle country in our stack.
Keep Latvia between Estonia and Lithuania. Riga and the gulf share a name, helping connect the cultural fact with the coastline.

states.name: Lithuania
lines: Lithuania is the southernmost Baltic country, below Latvia and above Poland and Belarus. Russia’s separate Kaliningrad territory lies along its southwestern side.
On March eleventh, 1990, Lithuania declared the restoration of its independence. That declaration became a defining moment in its departure from Soviet rule.
Finish the Baltic stack: Estonia at the top, Latvia in the middle, Lithuania at the bottom. Lithuania is the Baltic member nearest Poland.

states.name: Belarus
lines: Belarus is inland, east of Poland, below Lithuania and Latvia, and north of Ukraine. Russia lies along its eastern and northeastern side.
The Bialowieza Forest crosses the Belarus-Poland border. It preserves old forest habitat and supports European bison, linking this country to a living landscape rather than a coastline.
Remember Belarus above Ukraine and east of Poland. Picture the shared forest and bison on its western edge.
states.transition: Let's bring Belarus and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Ukraine
lines: Ukraine lies south of Belarus and west of Russia, with Black Sea shores to the south. Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Moldova connect it to central and southeastern Europe.
Kyiv was a major centre of medieval Kyivan Rus. Saint Sophia Cathedral and the city’s historic monastic sites preserve connections with that long history.
Keep Ukraine below Belarus and above the Black Sea. Kyiv is its historical anchor; current occupation does not change Ukraine’s internationally recognised borders.

states.name: Moldova
lines: Moldova is the narrow inland country between Romania and Ukraine. It comes close to the Black Sea region but has no sea coast.
Its Milestii Mici cellars occupy underground limestone galleries and hold a wine collection recognised by Guinness World Records. Imagine long tunnels of bottles under this small country.
Remember Moldova squeezed between Romania and Ukraine: an inland sliver, with underground wine cellars as its memory hook.
states.transition: Let's bring Moldova and its neighbours into a closer view.

states.name: Romania
lines: Romania lies west of Moldova and Ukraine’s southwestern side, and north of Bulgaria across the Danube. Its southeastern edge reaches the Black Sea.

Bran Castle is marketed as Dracula’s Castle, but Bram Stoker’s fictional castle and the historical ruler Vlad were different stories. A memorable legend should not replace the geography or the history.
Picture Romania above Bulgaria, with the Carpathian arc in its interior and a Black Sea opening on the east. Keep Dracula as a story, not a location guide.

states.name: Bulgaria
lines: Bulgaria lies directly below Romania, north of Greece and west of the Black Sea. Serbia and North Macedonia are its western neighbours, with Türkiye to the southeast.
The Cyrillic alphabet developed in the First Bulgarian Empire around the ninth and tenth centuries. Its later spread connects Bulgaria with many other languages using Cyrillic today.
Remember Bulgaria below Romania: the Danube helps divide the pair, and both reach the Black Sea. The alphabet is Bulgaria’s cultural memory hook.

states.name: Russia
lines: Russia extends far beyond this European view. Here we see its western part, east of Finland, the Baltic countries, Belarus and Ukraine; Kaliningrad is separate on the Baltic.
Its Lake Baikal is the world’s deepest lake, but lies in Siberia, in Asian Russia, outside this map view. A country can span two continents without becoming two countries.

Remember European Russia continuing off the eastern edge, and keep Kaliningrad separate from the main landmass. Our six-video route finishes here after forty-five places, including the six supplemental microstates.
states.transition: Let's bring Russia and its neighbours into a closer view.

recap: The Baltic stack is Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. Inland, Belarus is above Ukraine; Moldova fits between Ukraine and Romania, while Bulgaria sits below Romania along the Black Sea.

Russia continues far beyond Europe; its Siberian facts belong outside this European map view. Across six lessons we covered all thirty-nine GeoClick Europe targets, plus six microstates in labelled supplemental views.

This is the scope of our map-based series, not a universal definition of Europe. Türkiye, Cyprus and the Caucasus are outside this map’s target list and are left for neighbouring-region lessons. Rebuild the six groups using their locations and memorable facts.
